panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Human liver MRI showing hepatic parenchymal nodularity attributed by the caption to nodular regenerative hyperplasia and pseudocirrhosis in HHT. b: Human liver MRI showing a caption-described reticular peripheral fibrosis pattern associated with HHT; this specific finding is not represented in the allowed vocabulary. c: Delayed contrast-enhanced liver MRI in an HHT patient shows abnormal hepatic enhancement and multiple hepatic telangiectases, manifestations specifically attributed by the caption but not separately represented in the allowed vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Chronic liver injury with nodular regenerative hyperplasia, pseudocirrhosis, and peripheral fibrosis in a 54-year-old woman with HHT. (a) Axial T1-weighted MR image shows parenchymal nodularity most prominent in the posterior right hepatic lobe (arrow). (b) Axial T2-weighted fat-saturated MR image shows a reticular pattern of increased signal in the posterior right hepatic lobe (arrow). (c) Delayed enhancement on the axial T1 fat-saturated gadolinium-enhanced MR image (arrow), along with multiple telangiectases (arrowheads).
in_text_mentions: Alterations in liver blood flow caused by VMs in HHT can lead to either diffuse or focal hepatocellular regenerative activity, with fibrosis surrounding the abnormal vasculature [12]. On imaging, hepatic nodules and fibrosis mimic the appearance of cirrhosis. However, in HHT this appearance has been termed ‘‘pseudocirrhosis,’’ as the normal hepatocellular architecture is preserved (Figure 7) [12,16,36]. Unlike in true cirrhosis, there is not the same increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in pseudocirrhosis.

panels.rationale: The single panel is a real human-patient contrast-enhanced axial T1 MR image from a 51-year-old woman with HHT. It directly demonstrates an HHT-associated intrahepatic arterioportal shunt with early portal venous filling and an associated right hepatic lobe perfusion anomaly.
panels.attribution_text: Harwin et al. The Role of Liver Imaging in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia.. Journal of clinical medicine 2020. doi:10.3390/jcm9113750. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Arterioportal shunt from the hepatic artery to portal vein in a 51-year-old woman with HHT. Axial T1 MR image with fat saturation acquired during the arterial phase of contrast shows early filling of a right portal vein branch (arrow) adjacent to the dilated hepatic artery, and associated perfusion anomaly in the right hepatic lobe.
in_text_mentions: An arterioportal shunt occurs when the hepatic artery is in direct communication with the portal vein (Figure 3). In this type of shunt, the portal vein is exposed to high arterial pressures and also experiences increased blood flow. This leads to presinusoidal portal hypertension, which may lead to the development of ascites, varices, and splenomegaly [12,19].

panels.figure_caption: A 65-year-old female presented with chronic heart failure. Contrast-enhanced upper abdominal MRI and CT (A–G) showed multiple intrahepatic arteriovenous fistulas, a dilated hepatic artery (approximately 8.7 mm in diameter), tortuous and dilated portal and hepatic veins, and multiple intrahepatic perfusion abnormalities. Doppler ultrasound (H) revealed altered intrahepatic blood flow. The patient had a history of recurrent epistaxis, and physical examination showed scattered cutaneous petechiae. The patient is under ongoing follow-up.
in_text_mentions: ced MRI comprised hepatic arterial dilatation (approximately 8.7 mm in diameter), early opacification of the portal and hepatic veins during the arterial phase, diffuse abnormal hepatic perfusion, portal hypertension, and splenomegaly (Figures 1A–H). Physical examination revealed scattered cutaneous telangiectasias, and the patient reported a history of recurrent epistaxis, no family history. The diagnosis of HHT was confirmed based on clinical criteria. The patient is currently receiving symptomatic treatment for heart failure and undergoing regular follow-up examinations at a local hospital.
